subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: 9.1 Kinetic Theory of Temperature and Pressure

questions.q: A sealed box contains helium gas. Which description of the helium atoms explains why the gas exerts a steady outward force on every wall of the box?
options: Atoms at rest in fixed places repel one another, so the gas pushes out on each wall like a spring.
Atoms moving in random directions keep hitting each wall, and each collision pushes on it.
The atoms swell until together they fill the box, and so they press hard on each of its walls.
Heat stored in the helium pushes outward, so the gas presses on each wall of the box.
optionWhy: A student who pictures a gas as atoms held apart by repulsion picks this. Gas atoms are not at rest in fixed places; they move in random directions and exert forces only during collisions. The push on the walls comes from atoms colliding with them.

In the kinetic model the atoms move in random directions and collide with the walls. In each collision the wall exerts a force on the atom and the atom exerts an equal and opposite force on the wall. Very many collisions each second, on every wall, add up to a steady average outward force.

A student who gives atoms the properties of the bulk gas picks this. The atoms of a gas do not swell to fill the container; they are tiny compared with the spaces between them. They push on the walls because they move and collide with them.

A student who thinks of heat as a substance inside the gas picks this. The gas does not contain heat that pushes. Its pressure comes from its atoms colliding with the walls; heating the gas makes the atoms move faster, so they collide harder and more often.
questions.explain: In the kinetic model the atoms move in random directions and collide with the walls. In each collision the wall exerts a force on the atom and the atom exerts an equal and opposite force on the wall. Very many collisions each second, on every wall, add up to a steady average outward force.

questions.q: A container holds a mixture of 1.0 mol of helium and 3.0 mol of argon, both at the same temperature. An argon atom has about ten times the mass of a helium atom. Which quantity is the same for the helium as for the argon?
options: Average speed of the atoms
Total kinetic energy of its atoms
Kinetic energy of every atom
Average kinetic energy per atom
optionWhy: A student who thinks equal temperatures mean equal speeds picks this. Equal temperatures mean equal average kinetic energies; since K = (1/2)mv², the lighter helium atoms move faster on average, by a factor of about √10 ≈ 3.

A student who thinks temperature measures the total kinetic energy picks this. The average kinetic energy is the same, but there are three times as many argon atoms, so the argon has three times the total kinetic energy.

A student who thinks every atom at a given temperature has the same energy picks this. In each gas the atoms have a wide range of kinetic energies, as the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution shows; only the average is fixed by the temperature.

Temperature is characterized by the average kinetic energy of the atoms, K_avg = (3/2)k_B T. At the same temperature, helium and argon atoms have the same average kinetic energy, whatever their masses.
questions.explain: Temperature is characterized by the average kinetic energy of the atoms, K_avg = (3/2)k_B T. At the same temperature, helium and argon atoms have the same average kinetic energy, whatever their masses.

questions.q: The diagram shows, from above, a helium atom of mass 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg that strikes a fixed, smooth wall of its container with speed 1.20 × 10³ m/s and rebounds elastically with the same speed. The angles are marked on the diagram. What is the magnitude of the change in the atom's momentum during the collision?
optionWhy: A student who counts only the stopping part of the collision picks this: mv cos 60° = 3.98 × 10⁻²⁴. The wall first brings the perpendicular momentum to zero and then pushes the atom back out with the same perpendicular momentum in the opposite direction, so the change is twice as large.

A student who reverses the whole velocity picks this: 2mv = 1.59 × 10⁻²³, the result for a head-on collision. The atom strikes at an angle, and a smooth wall exerts no force parallel to itself, so only the perpendicular component, v cos 60°, reverses.

The smooth wall exerts a force only perpendicular to itself, so the component of velocity parallel to the wall is unchanged. The angle is measured from the normal, so the perpendicular component is v cos 60°; it reverses, from toward the wall to away from it. |Δp| = 2mv cos 60° = 2(6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg)(1.20 × 10³ m/s)(0.500) = 7.97 × 10⁻²⁴ kg·m/s.

A student who uses the sine picks this: 2mv sin 60° = 1.38 × 10⁻²³. The 60° angle is measured from the normal, so the component perpendicular to the wall is v cos 60°; v sin 60° is the component parallel to the wall, which does not change.
questions.explain: The smooth wall exerts a force only perpendicular to itself, so the component of velocity parallel to the wall is unchanged. The angle is measured from the normal, so the perpendicular component is v cos 60°; it reverses, from toward the wall to away from it. |Δp| = 2mv cos 60° = 2(6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg)(1.20 × 10³ m/s)(0.500) = 7.97 × 10⁻²⁴ kg·m/s.
questions.working: Perpendicular (normal) component of velocity: v cos 60° = (1.20 × 10³ m/s)(0.500) = 600 m/s, reversed by the collision; the parallel component v sin 60° is unchanged (smooth wall). |Δp| = 2mv cos 60° = 2(6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg)(600 m/s) = 7.968 × 10⁻²⁴ ≈ 7.97 × 10⁻²⁴ kg·m/s. Errors: stop only, mv cos 60° = 3.98 × 10⁻²⁴; whole velocity reversed, 2mv = 1.59 × 10⁻²³; sine for cosine, 2mv sin 60° = 1.38 × 10⁻²³.

questions.q: In a computer simulation of a gas, the atoms that strike one flat wall of the container during a time interval of 0.020 s deliver a total impulse of 2.0 × 10⁻² N·s to the wall, directed perpendicular to it. The wall has an area of 4.0 cm². What is the average pressure the gas exerts on the wall during this interval?
optionWhy: The average total perpendicular force is the impulse divided by the time interval: F = (2.0 × 10⁻² N·s)/(0.020 s) = 1.0 N. The area is 4.0 cm² = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ m². P = F_⊥/A = 1.0 N/(4.0 × 10⁻⁴ m²) = 2.5 × 10³ Pa.

A student who uses the impulse as if it were the force picks this: (2.0 × 10⁻² N·s)/(4.0 × 10⁻⁴ m²) = 5.0 × 10¹. Impulse is force multiplied by time, so the average force is the impulse divided by 0.020 s, which is 1.0 N.

A student who converts the area as if it were a length picks this, using 4.0 cm² = 4.0 × 10⁻² m²: 1.0 N/(4.0 × 10⁻² m²) = 2.5 × 10¹ Pa. Since 1 cm = 10⁻² m, 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m², so the area is 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ m².

A student who takes the total force on the wall as its pressure picks this: the average force is 1.0 N. Pressure is force per unit area, so the 1.0 N must be divided by the wall's area, 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ m².
questions.explain: The average total perpendicular force is the impulse divided by the time interval: F = (2.0 × 10⁻² N·s)/(0.020 s) = 1.0 N. The area is 4.0 cm² = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ m². P = F_⊥/A = 1.0 N/(4.0 × 10⁻⁴ m²) = 2.5 × 10³ Pa.
questions.working: F_⊥,avg = J/Δt = (2.0 × 10⁻² N·s)/(0.020 s) = 1.0 N. A = 4.0 cm² = 4.0 × (10⁻² m)² = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ m². P = F_⊥/A = 1.0 N/(4.0 × 10⁻⁴ m²) = 2.5 × 10³ Pa. Errors: impulse used as force, 2.0 × 10⁻²/4.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 5.0 × 10¹ Pa; area converted with 10⁻², 1.0/(4.0 × 10⁻²) = 2.5 × 10¹ Pa; force taken as pressure, 1.0 × 10⁰.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the assumptions of the classical model of an ideal gas?
options: The atoms exert appreciable forces on one another only while they collide.
The atoms lose a little kinetic energy in every collision with one another.
The atoms are packed so closely that they fill most of the gas's volume.
All the atoms move at one common speed, and in random directions.
optionWhy: The ideal-gas model assumes that the only appreciable forces on the atoms are those that occur during collisions. Between collisions each atom moves in a straight line at constant speed. (The model also assumes random velocities, negligible atomic volumes and elastic collisions.)
A student who thinks the motion of gas atoms runs down picks this. The model assumes that the collisions are elastic: kinetic energy passes from one atom to another, but the total is unchanged.

A student who pictures gas atoms as closely packed picks this. The model assumes the opposite: the volumes of the atoms are negligible compared with the volume the gas occupies, which is mostly empty space.

A student who thinks every atom has the same speed picks this. The model assumes random velocities, meaning a range of speeds as well as random directions; collisions keep changing the speed of each atom.
questions.explain: The ideal-gas model assumes that the only appreciable forces on the atoms are those that occur during collisions. Between collisions each atom moves in a straight line at constant speed. (The model also assumes random velocities, negligible atomic volumes and elastic collisions.)

questions.q: Students measure the pressure of three samples of gas, each sealed in a rigid container, at several temperatures between 0°C and 100°C. The samples are of different gases and different amounts, and each behaves as an ideal gas. For each sample they plot P against T in °C and get a straight line. They then extend each best-fit line to P = 0. What do they find?
options: All three lines reach P = 0 at the same temperature, 0°C.
All three lines reach P = 0 at the same temperature, about −273°C.
The steepest line reaches P = 0 at the highest temperature.
Each line reaches P = 0 at a temperature set by its kind of gas.
optionWhy: A student who takes 0°C to be the zero of temperature picks this. At 0°C the atoms are still moving and each gas still has a pressure; the lines reach P = 0 at about −273°C, which is 0 K.

For an ideal gas at constant volume, P = (nR/V)(T_C + 273), which is zero at T_C = −273°C whatever n, V or the kind of gas. The lines have different slopes, but all extrapolate to the same point on the temperature axis, absolute zero.
A student who judges where a line meets the axis by its slope alone picks this. The steeper lines also start at higher pressures, and every line reaches P = 0 at the same temperature, about −273°C.

A student who thinks the zero-pressure temperature is a property of each substance, like a boiling point, picks this. For every ideal gas the extrapolated temperature is the same, about −273°C, which is why it defines the zero of the Kelvin scale.
questions.explain: For an ideal gas at constant volume, P = (nR/V)(T_C + 273), which is zero at T_C = −273°C whatever n, V or the kind of gas. The lines have different slopes, but all extrapolate to the same point on the temperature axis, absolute zero.
questions.working: Ideal gas at constant volume: P = (nR/V)T with T = T_C + 273, so P = (nR/V)(T_C + 273), a straight line in T_C whose slope nR/V differs from sample to sample but which is zero at T_C = −273°C for every sample.

questions.q: In the ideal-gas model, a sample of gas is sealed in a rigid container whose walls let no energy in or out. The gas is left alone for a long time. Which claim about the average kinetic energy of its atoms, with its reasoning, is correct?
options: It decreases, since the atoms lose some energy in each collision and slow down.
It stays the same, since every collision, with an atom or a wall, is elastic.
It decreases, since pushing on the walls uses up some of the atoms' energy.
It increases, since collisions between the atoms produce heat, as friction does.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the motion of gas atoms runs down picks this. The collisions in the model are elastic, so the atoms do not lose kinetic energy in them; the gas keeps its temperature.

In the ideal-gas model every collision is elastic and the atoms exert no other appreciable forces, so collisions only pass kinetic energy from atom to atom. With no energy entering or leaving through the walls, the total kinetic energy, and so the average, stays the same indefinitely.
A student who thinks exerting a force uses up energy picks this. The walls are rigid and do not move, so the atoms' forces on them do no work and transfer no energy.
A student who thinks collisions generate heat picks this. The kinetic energy of the atoms is itself the thermal energy of the gas; elastic collisions pass it around without adding any.
questions.explain: In the ideal-gas model every collision is elastic and the atoms exert no other appreciable forces, so collisions only pass kinetic energy from atom to atom. With no energy entering or leaving through the walls, the total kinetic energy, and so the average, stays the same indefinitely.

questions.q: A rigid container of volume 10.0 L holds 0.500 mol of an ideal gas at 27°C. What is the pressure of the gas? Use R = 8.31 J/(mol·K) and 1 L = 1.00 × 10⁻³ m³.
optionWhy: A student who uses the Celsius temperature picks this: (0.500)(8.31)(27)/(1.00 × 10⁻²) = 1.12 × 10⁴. The gas law needs the absolute temperature, 300 K.
A student who substitutes the volume in liters picks this: (0.500)(8.31)(300)/10.0 = 1.25 × 10². With R in J/(mol·K), V must be in cubic meters: 10.0 L = 1.00 × 10⁻² m³.
A student who sets PV equal to the total kinetic energy of the atoms, (3/2)nRT, picks this: (3/2)(0.500)(8.31)(300)/(1.00 × 10⁻²) = 1.87 × 10⁵. The ideal gas law is PV = nRT, without the factor 3/2.

questions.q: Two systems are in thermal contact. Which statement must be true of them?
options: They are touching, so that their particles can collide at the boundary.
They are at different temperatures, so energy is flowing between them now.
Energy can be transferred between them by conduction, convection or radiation.
Matter lies between them, since no energy can ever be transferred across a vacuum.
optionWhy: A student who thinks thermal contact means touching picks this. Radiation transfers energy between systems that do not touch, such as the Sun and Earth, and those systems are in thermal contact.

A student who thinks thermal contact exists only while energy flows picks this. Systems at the same temperature can be in thermal contact; they are then in thermal equilibrium, with no net energy transfer.

Two systems are in thermal contact if they can transfer energy by thermal processes, which are conduction, convection and radiation. They need not touch, need not have matter between them and need not be at different temperatures; at equal temperatures they are in thermal contact with no net transfer.

A student who thinks nothing can cross empty space picks this. Radiation transfers energy across a vacuum, as it does from the Sun to Earth, so systems separated by a vacuum can be in thermal contact.
questions.explain: Two systems are in thermal contact if they can transfer energy by thermal processes, which are conduction, convection and radiation. They need not touch, need not have matter between them and need not be at different temperatures; at equal temperatures they are in thermal contact with no net transfer.

questions.q: A vacuum flask has double glass walls with a vacuum between them. Which statement explains how the vacuum layer helps keep hot coffee in the flask hot?
options: It stops conduction and convection across the gap, since both processes need matter.
It stops all three thermal processes, since energy cannot be transferred across a vacuum.
It stops heat rising out of the coffee, since heat naturally moves upward.
It stops the cold of the air outside from getting in and cooling the coffee.
optionWhy: Conduction needs particles to collide and convection needs a fluid to move, so neither can carry energy across a vacuum. Radiation can cross the vacuum, which is why the glass is usually silvered to reduce it.
A student who thinks nothing can cross empty space picks this. Radiation needs no material medium and does cross a vacuum, as sunlight does; the vacuum stops conduction and convection only.

A student who thinks heat itself rises picks this. Heat has no preferred direction; the vacuum surrounds the coffee on the sides and bottom and works by stopping conduction and convection in every direction.
A student who thinks of cold as something that flows in picks this. The coffee cools because energy leaves it; the vacuum slows that by stopping conduction and convection across the gap.
questions.explain: Conduction needs particles to collide and convection needs a fluid to move, so neither can carry energy across a vacuum. Radiation can cross the vacuum, which is why the glass is usually silvered to reduce it.

questions.q: A hot apple pie is set on a counter in a cooler kitchen. Which statement about the pie, with its reasoning, is correct?
options: The pie is cooled, since cold is transferred into it from the counter and the air.
The pie is cooled, since energy is transferred out of it by thermal processes.
The pie is cooled, since the energy it loses is used up and ceases to exist.
The pie is heated, since it is the pie that gives out energy to its surroundings.
optionWhy: A student who thinks of cold as something that flows picks this. Nothing called cold enters the pie; the pie cools because energy leaves it for the cooler counter and air.

Cooling is the transfer of energy out of a system by thermal processes. The pie is at a higher temperature than the counter and the air, so energy leaves it by conduction, convection and radiation; the pie is cooled and its surroundings are heated.
A student who thinks energy is used up picks this. The energy the pie loses is not destroyed: the counter and the air gain exactly as much, and warm slightly.

A student who attaches 'heating' to the object that gives out energy picks this. Heating means energy transferred into a system. Energy leaves the pie, so the pie is cooled; the counter and air are heated.
questions.explain: Cooling is the transfer of energy out of a system by thermal processes. The pie is at a higher temperature than the counter and the air, so energy leaves it by conduction, convection and radiation; the pie is cooled and its surroundings are heated.

questions.q: A small hot metal block is lowered into a large tank of cold water. At the surface of the block, atoms of the metal collide with molecules of the water. Which statement about the energy transferred in these collisions is correct?
options: Energy passes from the metal atom to the water molecule in every single collision, as the metal is hotter.
No energy passes either way, since in an elastic collision each particle keeps its own kinetic energy.
Energy is more likely to pass from the water molecule to the metal atom, since the water has more internal energy.
Energy is more likely to pass from the more energetic particle to the less energetic one, though not in every collision.
optionWhy: A student who thinks every particle of the hotter system is more energetic than every particle of the colder one picks this. Both systems have wide ranges of particle energies, so some water molecules are more energetic than some metal atoms, and in their collisions energy goes to the metal.

A student who thinks each particle keeps its kinetic energy in an elastic collision picks this. Elastic means the total kinetic energy is conserved, not that each particle keeps its own; energy usually passes from one particle to the other.

A student who thinks energy flows from the system with more internal energy picks this. The large tank of water may well have more internal energy than the block, but the direction of net transfer is set by temperature: the metal's atoms have the greater average kinetic energy, so energy is more likely to pass from a metal atom to a water molecule.

In a collision between two particles, energy is most likely to be transferred from the particle with more kinetic energy to the one with less. The metal's atoms have the greater average kinetic energy, so over very many collisions the net transfer is into the water, although some individual collisions transfer energy the other way.
questions.explain: In a collision between two particles, energy is most likely to be transferred from the particle with more kinetic energy to the one with less. The metal's atoms have the greater average kinetic energy, so over very many collisions the net transfer is into the water, although some individual collisions transfer energy the other way.

questions.q: A copper block rests on a laboratory bench at room temperature. Which of the following makes up the internal energy of the block?
options: The kinetic energy of its vibrating atoms, without any potential energy of their arrangement
The heat stored in the block, which it gives out when it is placed next to a colder object
The kinetic energy of its vibrating atoms plus the potential energy of their arrangement
The block's gravitational potential energy on the bench plus the kinetic energy of the whole block
optionWhy: A student who thinks internal energy is only the random kinetic energy of the particles picks this. That is true of an ideal gas, whose atoms exert no conservative forces on one another, but the atoms of a solid are held in place by such forces, so the block's internal energy also includes the potential energy of their arrangement.

A student who thinks of heat as something an object contains picks this. Heating is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; it is not stored as heat. What the block contains is internal energy, the kinetic and potential energy of its atoms, which heating or cooling can change.

Internal energy is the sum of the kinetic energies of the objects that make up the system (here, copper atoms vibrating about their positions) and the potential energy of their configuration, which comes from the forces the atoms exert on one another.

A student who counts the energy of the block as a whole picks this. The gravitational potential energy belongs to the block–Earth system and depends on the block's position, and the kinetic energy of the whole block depends on the motion of its center of mass; neither is internal energy, which concerns the atoms' motion and arrangement relative to one another.
questions.explain: Internal energy is the sum of the kinetic energies of the objects that make up the system (here, copper atoms vibrating about their positions) and the potential energy of their configuration, which comes from the forces the atoms exert on one another.

questions.q: A sealed container of ideal gas rests on a level table. The container is heated, and the temperature of the gas increases. Which statement describes the gas and the container after the heating?
options: The container starts to move, as its gas has gained kinetic energy.
The gas atoms keep their average speed, but the gas now holds more heat.
The gas atoms move faster on average, and the container stays at rest.
The container now weighs less, as the gas in it is heated and hot gas rises.
optionWhy: A student who thinks that the kinetic energy gained by the atoms must appear as motion of the whole object picks this. The atoms move in random directions, so their extra kinetic energy is internal energy; with no net external horizontal force, the center of mass stays at rest.

A student who thinks heat is a substance stored alongside the atoms picks this. The energy transferred by heating becomes internal energy, which for an ideal gas is the kinetic energy of its atoms, so their average speed must increase as the temperature rises.

Heating increases the internal energy of the gas, which for an ideal gas is the kinetic energy of its atoms moving randomly relative to one another: a higher temperature means a greater average kinetic energy. The random motions add to zero net momentum, so the center of mass of the gas and container stays at rest.

A student who thinks heated gas weighs less because hot air rises picks this. Hot air rises through cooler air because it is less dense; the sealed container holds the same mass of gas before and after heating, so its weight is unchanged.
questions.explain: Heating increases the internal energy of the gas, which for an ideal gas is the kinetic energy of its atoms moving randomly relative to one another: a higher temperature means a greater average kinetic energy. The random motions add to zero net momentum, so the center of mass of the gas and container stays at rest.

questions.q: A 2.0 kg copper block at 80°C and a 1.0 kg copper block at 20°C are placed in contact inside an insulated box, and the two blocks form an isolated system. They reach the same final temperature. Which statement about the energy of the blocks is correct?
options: The blocks' total energy has fallen, as some was used up in the transfer.
The total energy of the two blocks is the same afterward as it was beforehand.
The two blocks end with equal internal energies, as they have equal temperatures.
The cold block keeps the same energy, and its cold passes into the hot block.
optionWhy: A student who thinks energy is used up when it is transferred picks this. Energy is conserved: in an isolated system none can be lost, so all of the energy lost by the hotter block is gained by the colder block.

The two blocks form an isolated system, so their total energy is constant. Energy is transferred from the hotter block to the colder one until their temperatures are equal: the internal energy lost by the 2.0 kg block equals the internal energy gained by the 1.0 kg block.

A student who thinks equal temperatures mean equal internal energies picks this. Temperature is related to the average kinetic energy per atom; the 2.0 kg block has twice as many atoms at the same final temperature, so it has more internal energy.

A student who thinks of cold as something that flows picks this. Energy is transferred from the hotter block to the colder block; the colder block's temperature rises because its internal energy increases.
questions.explain: The two blocks form an isolated system, so their total energy is constant. Energy is transferred from the hotter block to the colder one until their temperatures are equal: the internal energy lost by the 2.0 kg block equals the internal energy gained by the 1.0 kg block.

questions.q: A gas in a cylinder is compressed by a piston. During the compression, 250 J of work is done on the gas, and 400 J of energy is transferred from the gas to its surroundings by cooling. What is the change in the internal energy of the gas?
optionWhy: ΔU = Q + W. The work done on the gas is W = +250 J, and energy leaving by cooling makes Q = −400 J. ΔU = −400 J + 250 J = −150 J: the gas loses more energy by cooling than it gains as work.
A student who takes W as the work done by the gas picks this: W = −250 J gives ΔU = −400 J − 250 J = −650 J. In ΔU = Q + W, W is the work done on the gas, +250 J for a compression.
A student who adds the two energy transfers without signs picks this: 400 J + 250 J = 650 J. Energy leaving the gas by cooling makes Q negative, −400 J.
A student who counts only the energy transferred by cooling picks this. The 250 J of work done on the gas is also a transfer of energy into it, which makes up part of the 400 J lost.
questions.explain: ΔU = Q + W. The work done on the gas is W = +250 J, and energy leaving by cooling makes Q = −400 J. ΔU = −400 J + 250 J = −150 J: the gas loses more energy by cooling than it gains as work.
questions.working: ΔU = Q + W. W = +250 J (work done on the gas); Q = −400 J (energy leaves by cooling). ΔU = −400 J + 250 J = −150 J.

questions.q: A 0.200 kg aluminum block is heated from 20.0°C to 60.0°C. The specific heat of aluminum is 900 J/(kg·K). How much energy is transferred to the block?
optionWhy: A student who puts the final temperature, 60.0°C, in place of the temperature change picks this: (0.200 kg)(900 J/(kg·K))(60.0) = 1.1 × 10⁴ J. Q = mcΔT needs the change, 40.0 K.
The temperature change is ΔT = 60.0°C − 20.0°C = 40.0 K; a change of one Celsius degree is a change of one kelvin. Q = mcΔT = (0.200 kg)(900 J/(kg·K))(40.0 K) = 7.2 × 10³ J.
A student who adds 273 to the temperature change picks this, using ΔT = 313 K. Adding 273 converts a temperature, not a difference: a rise of 40.0°C is a rise of 40.0 K.

A student who treats the specific heat as the energy needed to warm the whole block by 1 K picks this, leaving out the mass: (900 J/(kg·K))(40.0 K). Specific heat is energy per kilogram per kelvin, so it must be multiplied by the mass, 0.200 kg.
questions.explain: The temperature change is ΔT = 60.0°C − 20.0°C = 40.0 K; a change of one Celsius degree is a change of one kelvin. Q = mcΔT = (0.200 kg)(900 J/(kg·K))(40.0 K) = 7.2 × 10³ J.

questions.q: The specific heat of liquid water is about twice the specific heat of ice. Which statement best accounts for this difference?
options: Liquid water is denser than ice, so each kilogram of it contains more molecules.
Freezing changes how the molecules interact, so the energy per kilogram per kelvin changes.
Liquid water is warmer than ice, so it contains more heat to begin with.
Liquid water conducts energy better than ice, so it takes in more energy.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a denser material packs more molecules into each kilogram picks this. Density is mass per unit volume; a kilogram of ice and a kilogram of liquid water contain the same number of molecules, because every water molecule has the same mass.

Specific heat is an intrinsic property that depends on how a material's atoms or molecules are arranged and interact. Ice and liquid water are the same substance, but freezing changes the arrangement of the molecules and how they interact, so each phase has its own specific heat.

A student who thinks of heat as something an object contains picks this. Specific heat is the energy needed per kilogram per kelvin of temperature change, not energy stored in a sample, and ice and liquid water can both be at 0°C.

A student who treats thermal conductivity and specific heat as one property picks this. Conductivity describes how fast energy passes through a material; specific heat describes how much energy a kilogram needs per kelvin. In fact ice conducts better than liquid water.
questions.explain: Specific heat is an intrinsic property that depends on how a material's atoms or molecules are arranged and interact. Ice and liquid water are the same substance, but freezing changes the arrangement of the molecules and how they interact, so each phase has its own specific heat.

questions.q: A 0.300 kg iron block at 80.0°C is placed in 0.500 kg of water at 20.0°C in an insulated container, and the block and the water reach a common temperature. The specific heat of iron is 450 J/(kg·K), and the specific heat of water is 4180 J/(kg·K). Energy transfer to the container and the surroundings is negligible. What is the common temperature?
optionWhy: A student who takes the common temperature to be halfway between the starting temperatures picks this. That holds only when the two objects have equal values of mc; here the water's mc is about 15 times the iron's, so the common temperature is much closer to 20.0°C.

A student who weights the two temperatures by mass alone picks this, as if a kilogram of iron and a kilogram of water needed the same energy per kelvin. Their specific heats differ by a factor of more than 9, and the energy balance must include them.

A student who thinks the material with the greater specific heat changes temperature more picks this: in effect the two specific heats are swapped, so the water warms by about 51 K while the iron cools by only about 9 K. The reverse is true: water's large specific heat keeps its temperature change small.

The energy transferred from the iron equals the energy transferred to the water: (0.300 kg)(450 J/(kg·K))(80.0°C − T) = (0.500 kg)(4180 J/(kg·K))(T − 20.0°C), which gives T = 23.6°C. The water, with much the larger mc, changes temperature much less than the iron.
questions.explain: The energy transferred from the iron equals the energy transferred to the water: (0.300 kg)(450 J/(kg·K))(80.0°C − T) = (0.500 kg)(4180 J/(kg·K))(T − 20.0°C), which gives T = 23.6°C. The water, with much the larger mc, changes temperature much less than the iron.

questions.q: A copper rod, insulated along its sides, connects two reservoirs held at different temperatures, and energy is conducted along it at a steady rate. The rod is replaced by a copper rod of the same length but twice the diameter, and the temperature difference between the reservoirs is halved. By what factor does the rate of energy transfer along the rod change?
options: ×½
×⅛
optionWhy: A student who doubles the area when the diameter doubles picks this: 2 × ½ = 1. The area of a circle is πd²/4, so doubling the diameter makes it four times as great.

A student who thinks the rate does not depend on the rod's cross-sectional area picks this, counting only the halved temperature difference. A wider rod provides more paths for conduction: the rate is proportional to A.
Q/Δt = kAΔT/L. The cross-sectional area is proportional to the square of the diameter, so doubling the diameter makes the area 4 times as great. Halving ΔT halves the rate: 4 × ½ = 2.
A student who puts the area underneath and the length on top picks this: (1/4) × (1/2) = 1/8. In Q/Δt = kAΔT/L the area is in the numerator: a wider rod conducts energy faster.
questions.explain: Q/Δt = kAΔT/L. The cross-sectional area is proportional to the square of the diameter, so doubling the diameter makes the area 4 times as great. Halving ΔT halves the rate: 4 × ½ = 2.
questions.working: Q/Δt = kAΔT/L. A = πd²/4, so d → 2d gives A → 4A; ΔT → ΔT/2; k and L unchanged. Factor = 4 × ½ = 2. (Area ∝ d: 2 × ½ = 1. Area ignored: ½. L/A instead of A/L: ¼ × ½ = ⅛.)
